result.question: Trace the evolution of bronze sculpture in India from the Harappan period to the Chola age. (Answer in 150 words)

sentences.text: India's bronze tradition rests on the lost-wax or cire-perdue process, known since the Indus Valley Civilisation.
The Dancing Girl from Mohenjodaro is among the earliest surviving bronze figures.
Kushana-period images of Jain tirthankaras come from Chausa in Bihar.
A famous hoard of Buddhist bronzes found at Akota near Vadodara shows that casting flourished in Gujarat.
Gupta and post-Gupta standing Buddhas, such as the monumental Sultanganj image from Bihar, show a refined classical style with foldless drapery.
Himachal and Kashmir produced distinctive images such as the four-headed Vaikuntha Vishnu, while Pala workshops at Nalanda and Kurkihar revived the Gupta idiom.
Bronze casting reached its peak under the Cholas, with queen Sembiyan Mahadevi as a notable patron.
The Chola Nataraja balances on his left leg, crushing the dwarf Apasmara, while his raised right leg signifies release from illusion.
Kumbakonam artisans still practise this craft, and supporting such living traditions can sustain both heritage and livelihoods.
